Post-Mastectomy Care Guide — Recovery, Scar Care, and Bras

Evidence-based post-mastectomy recovery guide: scar care timeline, lymphedema prevention, gentle exercises, and the best bras to wear at each healing stage.

The Recovery Timeline

Recovery from mastectomy varies based on the type of surgery (simple, skin-sparing, nipple-sparing, or modified radical), whether reconstruction was performed, and individual healing. The following is a general week-by-week guide. Always follow your surgeon's specific instructions[1].

Weeks 1–2: Immediate Post-Surgery

  • Surgical drains are typically in place for 7–14 days; your care team will teach you how to empty and measure them.
  • Wear the post-surgical compression bra provided by your hospital, day and night. This bra has front closure and no underwire.
  • Limit arm movement to below shoulder height. Avoid lifting anything heavier than a phone or a cup of tea.
  • Pain management: prescribed analgesics for the first 1–2 weeks, transitioning to over-the-counter pain relief as needed.

Weeks 3–4: Early Healing

  • Drains are usually removed.
  • Incisions begin to close. Watch for signs of infection: increased redness, warmth, swelling, or discharge.
  • Gentle range-of-motion exercises begin (pendulum swings, wall walks). Your surgeon may refer you to a physical therapist.
  • Continue wearing the post-surgical bra or transition to a soft, front-closure mastectomy bra.

Weeks 5–8: Mobility Returns

  • Most women return to light daily activities. Driving is usually safe once you are off opioid pain medications and can move the arms comfortably.
  • Incisions are mostly healed. Begin scar care (see below).
  • Light exercise (walking, gentle yoga) is typically approved.
  • If you are being fitted for a permanent prosthesis, this is the typical time frame.

Weeks 9–12: Building Strength

  • Most surgeons clear you for full activity, including swimming, cycling, and moderate strength training.
  • Continue gentle breast and chest wall stretches to prevent capsular contracture (after reconstruction).
  • Follow up with your surgical team for any concerns about healing, sensation, or implant position (if applicable).

Scar Care

Once the incisions are fully closed (typically 3–4 weeks post-surgery), begin a scar care routine. The goal is to keep the scar soft, flat, and flexible[2].

1. Silicone Sheeting or Gel

Medical-grade silicone applied to the scar for 12–24 hours per day, for 3–6 months, is the gold-standard non-invasive scar treatment. It hydrates the scar tissue and reduces thickness and redness.

2. Gentle Massage

Once the incision is fully closed, gentle circular massage with a vitamin E or silicone-based cream helps break down collagen adhesions. Use light pressure for 5–10 minutes, twice daily.

3. Sun Protection

Fresh scars are highly sensitive to UV radiation. Cover the scar with clothing or use SPF 30+ sunscreen for at least 12 months after surgery to prevent permanent darkening.

4. Avoid Tension

Wear a supportive bra day and night for the first 6–8 weeks to prevent tension on the incision lines, which can widen the scar.

Lymphedema Prevention

Lymphedema — swelling of the arm, hand, or chest wall on the surgical side — is a potential complication after axillary lymph node removal or radiation. Risk is highest in the first 2–3 years after surgery. Prevention strategies:

  • Avoid blood draws, blood pressure cuffs, and injections on the surgical arm when possible.
  • Wear a compression sleeve during air travel or strenuous activity (your surgeon will advise).
  • Treat any skin break (cut, scrape, insect bite) on the surgical arm promptly with antiseptic to prevent infection.
  • Maintain a healthy weight; obesity is a major lymphedema risk factor.
  • Begin gentle range-of-motion exercises as soon as your surgeon clears you.

Gentle Exercises for Recovery

The following exercises are typically started 1–2 weeks after surgery. Stop any exercise that causes sharp pain or pulling at the incision[3].

1. Pendulum Swings

Bend forward at the waist, allowing the surgical arm to hang loose. Gently swing the arm in small circles (10 each direction), then forward and back (10 reps), then side to side (10 reps). Perform twice daily.

2. Wall Walks

Stand facing a wall, about 15 cm away. Walk your fingers up the wall as high as is comfortable, hold for 5 seconds, and walk them back down. Repeat 5–10 times, twice daily. Goal: full arm extension by week 4.

3. Shoulder Rolls

Seated or standing, slowly roll the shoulders forward in 10 circles, then backward in 10 circles. This prevents stiffness in the shoulder capsule.

4. Elbow Flexion

With the arm at your side, slowly bend the elbow to touch the shoulder, then straighten. Repeat 10 times per arm, twice daily.

FAQs

When can I shower after surgery?

Most surgeons allow gentle showering 48–72 hours after surgery, with the incision patted dry (not rubbed). Baths, hot tubs, and swimming are typically off-limits until the incision is fully closed (3–4 weeks).

When can I return to work?

Desk work is usually possible 2–4 weeks after surgery. Physically demanding jobs may require 6–8 weeks. Discuss your specific situation with your surgeon.

Will I have normal sensation in the breast area?

Sensation changes are common after mastectomy. Numbness, tingling, hypersensitivity, or shooting pains in the chest wall, incision line, or upper arm can persist for 6–12 months. Most women find that sensation gradually returns, though it may never be identical to the preoperative baseline.
